newsitem.title: MEXICO: Airbus sets sights on Boeing in Latam.
newsitem.headline: Airbus sets sights on Boeing in Latam.

text.p: In the battle of the world's two great commercial aircraft makers, Airbus Industrie considers Latin America to be ripe for the picking from market leader Boeing Co, a top Airbus official said on Friday.

"I've seen that lately the competition has a total lack of interest in the countries of Latin America," Rafael Alonso, the Airbus vice president for sales in Latin America and the Caribbean, told Reuters. "They feel they are conquered countries. It's their backyard."

Clearly, Airbus has a long way to go. Alonso said 10 airlines were currently operating 60 of its aircraft in Latin America and the Caribbean. By contrast, 50 airlines were operating 842 Boeing aircraft in the region at the end of 1995, company officials said.

Airbus, which says it has more than 40 percent of the world market, is a consortium involving France's Aerospatiale, British Aerospace, Germany's Daimler-Benz Aerospace and Spain's Casa. Boeing, which claims 64 percent of the world market, is based in Seattle.
Alonso made note of Boeing's lack of presence here at Aeroexpo '97, an international trade show and convention focusing on Latin America being held at the Acapulco Convention Center in Mexico.
Airbus has the largest display stand of the 97 companies in the convention, with a host of company officials pressing the flesh. Boeing has no display and sent only one public relations manager.

"The timing just wasn't right for us," Boeing spokeswoman Liz Verdier said by telephone from Seattle. "We didn't have any equipment available to send down. But we're expecting big things of Latin America. We have relationships with customers going back 30 years."
The Latin American market is small compared with other emerging markets such as Asia, though the region is seen as having high growth potential.

Alonso said Airbus provided 75 percent of all of the aircraft sold to Latin American and Caribbean airlines last year, a trend that has held for several years. Airbus expects to add another 10 airlines to its client base in the next five years.

Indeed, the consortium sees a booming market ahead in Latin America, where some 600 new jetliners are expected to be needed during the next 20 years. Half of them would replace an ageing fleet dominated by Boeing aircraft.
"They (airlines) are going to have to make a decision in the short term" about buying replacement aircraft, Alonso said.

Airbus believes its has just the product to capture a growing share of the replacement orders -- the A319. The newest and smallest aircraft in its line, the A319 is specially made for "hot and high" airports, that is, those situated at high altitudes or where hot weather prevails, as is the case in much of the region.

Boeing counters with the 737, of which there are 205 in Latin America. The U.S. company says the 737 is an ideal "hot and high" aircraft, particularly the later models such as the 737-600, 737-700 and 737-800.
Boeing also sees the potential in the region, but measures it in dollar terms -- $44 billion worth over the next 20 years, according to Tim Meskill, Boeing's director of world market forecasts.
He said many of the aircraft to be sold in Latin America were likely to be equipment previously used in the United States that will fail to meet noise standards taking effect in 1999.
"Latin America, for growth, is shaping up as the fastest- growing market in the world," Meskill said in a telephone interview. "We are far more encouraged in the past because of potential growth."
